EXTRA CLASS · KIDS GAMES

Every game, with its rules on the card.

The afternoon-saver class: twenty-six classic games walk the whole day in tour order — throwing and aiming, running and freezing, table games and turns, quiet find-and-solve games, acting and guessing, and the sidewalk classics — and every tile below opens its own simple how-to-play guide a kid can follow.

HOW THIS CLASS WORKS

Every game a childhood needs — with the rules on the card.

The Kids Games class is a bonus class, kept beside the main learning path like the Kitchen Helper and the Doctor Visit: the regular classes stay the core sequence, and this one is for the afternoons when somebody says I don’t know what to play. Twenty-six classic games — balloon keep-up, hide and seek, tic-tac-toe, treasure hunt — each one on its own card, and each card opens a simple guide a kid can follow: what you need, how to play, step by step, and one way to make it fresh tomorrow.

The games run in tour order on purpose. The throwing and rolling games come first, because aiming is where little arms start; then the running-and-freezing games that empty a room of wiggles; then the table games that teach waiting a turn; the quiet find-and-solve games for the rainy shelf; the acting games for loud imaginations; and the last group belongs outside — chalk, pavement and a rope on a swing.

THE GAMES, SIX WAYS TO PLAY

Twenty-six cards, six kinds of play.

Twenty-six games in six groups, in the order a real game afternoon unfolds. Tap any picture and it opens its own how-to-play guide — the original card on the left, and the simple kid-followable steps on the right.

Throw, roll & aim

Games where something flies: the balloon that must stay up, the beanbag, the ball, the rings and the paper plane — and the target waiting for every throw.

Balloon Keep-UpBeanbag TossBowlingHoop TossPaper Plane Target
Run, chase & freeze

The big-movement classics: hiding and seeking, freezing mid-dance, passing fast, walking the chairs and stopping on a word.

Duck, Duck, GooseFollow the LeaderFreeze DanceHide and SeekHot PotatoMusical ChairsRed Light, Green Light
Table & take turns

Sit-down games that teach waiting your turn: grids and discs, cards and pairs, a magnetic pond and one very decisive hand game.

BingoFishingFour in a RowMemory MatchRock, Paper, ScissorsTic-Tac-Toe
Look, find & solve

The quiet-power games: tracing mazes, joining pieces, catching the sneaky changes and following the clues to the treasure.

MazePuzzleSpot the DifferenceTreasure Hunt
Act, guess & listen

Games your imagination runs: acting without a single word and obeying only the commands that carry the magic words.

CharadesSimon Says
Playground & outdoors

The sidewalk classics: chalk numbers under hopping feet and a rope that keeps swinging to its own chant.

HopscotchJump Rope
THE CLASS GAME

Game Day: let the stack decide.

Stack the cards face down. Draw the top one, read its guide together, play the game — and the winner of each game draws the next card. That is Game Day, and it runs itself: the stack decides everything, the winning gets a crown (and the drawing job), and the afternoon ends only when the stack ends. Losing practice is built right in: short rounds, loud good-games, immediate rematches.

SAME GAME, TWO NAMES

Tic-tac-toe and noughts and crosses. Both are right.

Games travel lighter than words do — the same game grows a new name on every shore, and this class says so out loud. Tic-tac-toe is noughts and crosses in the UK; the jump rope is a skipping rope; the paper plane flies as a paper aeroplane; freeze dance is musical statues across the ocean; the balloon game rides the UK playground word keepy-uppy; and the disc-dropping grid most homes call Connect Four is simply four in a row here — the generic name, playable with buttons on a drawn grid. Whichever your family says, your child hears both — and learns early that games, like words, come in kinds.

SUPPORTING RESOURCE

Print the kids-games cards.

Every guide has a matching flashcard in the library: the original artwork as a printable card with a download button and short notes for grown-ups. Keep the five sit-down cards in a basket near the couch — on a gray afternoon, the basket is the plan.

New rule cards for the deck live on their own shelf at /games/ — one short page per game with the three rules printed on the card, what you need and a fresh twist: Duck Duck Goose, Hopscotch, Simon Says, Tag and thirty-one more.

Age ranges are a guide, not a test. Start with the game your child loves best, follow the giggle, follow the child — and say the rule out loud before every game: a child who can say the rule can run the game with friends.
